analysis.one_liner: Caps nationwide greenhouse gas emissions and auctions permits, returning proceeds as consumer rebates and community investments.
analysis.headline: The Climate Pollution Standard and Community Investment Act was introduced in December 2025 with zero cosponsors and referred to four House committees, none of which has acted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the Clean Air Act to put a declining national limit on greenhouse gas emissions, covering power plants of 25 megawatts or more, producers and importers of oil, coal-based fuels, and natural gas liquids, large industrial plants, and big gas utilities. Companies must surrender an allowance for every ton they emit, and most allowances are sold at quarterly auctions starting at a $15 minimum price that rises 5 percent plus inflation each year. The auction proceeds and free allowances are channeled to consumer rebates, state energy programs, low-income bill assistance, workers displaced by the energy transition, and communities that live near polluting facilities — where covered facilities would be allowed to emit only half a ton per allowance.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households, especially low-income consumers, who would receive rebates and bill assistance funded by auction proceeds; workers in fossil-dependent communities through a Worker and Community Assistance Fund; and people living near polluting plants, which would face a doubled compliance cost in designated Cleaner Air Communities.

how_it_helps.text: Sets enforceable targets for covered entities: at least 5 percent below the 2023–2025 average in 2027, no more than 50 percent of 2005 emissions by 2030, 30 percent by 2040, and 10 percent by 2050, with annual declines of at least 2 percent of 2005 emissions beginning in 2028.

Auctions 15 percent of allowances each year with proceeds going to the Treasury for a Clean Energy Rebate Program, and gives states an additional 30 percent of allowances (declining over time) to sell and spend on energy efficiency, low-emission alternatives, and direct assistance including low-income ratepayer relief.

Sends 5 percent of allowances to a Worker and Community Assistance Fund and 10 percent to a Cleaner Air Community Fund for frontline communities; facilities located in designated Cleaner Air Communities must surrender two allowances per ton instead of one.

Requires prevailing wages for laborers and mechanics on projects funded by allowance proceeds, and creates a full Title II program of transition studies, community hubs, and assistance for adversely affected workers and communities.

Sets a rising auction floor price — $15 per ton in 2027, plus 5 percent and inflation each year — and imposes civil penalties of three times the auction clearing price for any ton a company fails to cover.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, coal, chemical, cement, steel, and utility companies that exceed 25,000 tons of emissions per year, which would have to buy or earn allowances for every ton; some of those costs could be passed on to consumers through higher fuel and electricity prices, though rebates and state allocations are designed to offset that.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy industry

drawbacks.text: Fossil fuel producers and utilities would face new compliance costs and could pass them through to consumers in higher fuel and power prices before rebates arrive.

The bill creates a large tradable market in emission allowances, open to any buyer subject to a 5 percent per-auction purchase cap, and adds banking of allowances, which would require new market oversight and could allow financial speculation.

Energy-intensive, trade-exposed industries such as steel, cement, and aluminum would receive free output-based allowances — 15 percent of the cap at first — which protects them from foreign competition but softens their incentive to cut emissions and shrinks auction revenue for the consumer programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a hard, enforceable emissions cap with rebates and assistance aimed squarely at households and affected workers, and its design features — rising price floor, penalties at triple the clearing price, doubled compliance cost in overburdened communities — are stronger than typical cap-and-trade proposals. Its main real costs are potential near-term energy price increases and the free allowances carved out for trade-exposed industry, which reduce both the price signal and the revenue available for consumer programs. It never advanced far enough for its practical effects to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced days before the holiday recess and referred to four House committees, and none of those committees has held a hearing, markup, or vote on it since.

narrative.text: Representative Paul Tonko introduced the bill on December 19, 2025, near the end of the first session of the 119th Congress.
No member from either party signed on as a cosponsor.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Workforce, and Science, Space, and Technology committees, and no committee has taken further action on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the oil, gas, coal, and heavy-industry companies that would be covered by the emissions cap avoid the new costs, because no committee has moved the bill toward a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred; the only sign of support is a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors, while the four committees holding the bill are all chaired by Republicans.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and coal producers and importers
industries.note: Their products would be charged for the emissions from combustion — an allowance per ton with a rising auction floor — directly raising the cost of selling fossil fuels. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against the cleaner air and rebates ordinary people would get.

Plants of 25 megawatts or more would need allowances for every ton, but states may transfer allowances to them for the benefit of consumers, cushioning compliance costs. Their customers would receive rebates and efficiency programs funded from the same system.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive, trade-exposed manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals)
industries.note: They are covered emitters, but the bill gives them free output-based allowances — 15 percent of the cap at first, phasing down over 30 years — to keep them from moving production abroad. The protections blunt their costs but also reduce auction revenue for consumer programs.

industries.industry: Clean energy, efficiency, and negative-emissions industries
industries.note: State grants, an Energy Innovation Fund, and a growing Negative Emissions Activities Fund (reaching 20 percent of allowances after 30 years) would fund wind, solar, storage, efficiency, and carbon removal — creating customers for these industries at public expense. Their gains come alongside the bill's benefits to consumers.

Auctions would be open to any buyer and allowances would be freely tradable and bankable, creating a new commodity market of the scale of the entire covered economy. The bill adds oversight, beneficial-ownership disclosure, and a 5 percent per-auction purchase cap, but the market would still be a new profit center.

analysis.trajectory: A cap-and-trade bill with zero cosponsors, introduced at the very end of a session under full Republican control of the House and the committees holding it, almost never reaches the floor. Barring a dramatic change in cosponsorship or committee interest, the most likely path is that it sits without a hearing or markup until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
